appraisal_events.evidence: "ce n'est pas ce que nous appelons une comédienne de la grande lignée"; "vous n'avez imaginé quelque chose de plus risible"; "Je ne peux pas comprendre... comment Robert a jamais pu l'aimer."
appraisal_events.explanation: The duc and duchesse mock as absurd and unworthy the actress Robert once loved, and the duchesse voices open puzzlement at his taste, mildly discrediting Robert by association even as she folds the remark into a generalizing reflection on love's mystery.

appraisal_events.evidence: "dont le bizarre vocabulaire permettait à la fois aux gens du monde de dire qu'il n'était pas un sot et aux gens de lettres de le trouver le pire des imbéciles"
appraisal_events.explanation: The narrator's aside undercuts the duc's remark by noting that his idiosyncratic vocabulary only spares him from folly in society's eyes, while men of letters judge him the worst of imbeciles.

status_effects.explanation: Robert's judgment is mildly discredited through the couple's mockery of the woman he loved, though the duchesse's closing reflection on love's inherent mystery partly softens the blame.
The narrator's ironic gloss on the duc's peculiar vocabulary leaves him diminished, since the sharper of the two judgments reported is that lettered people find him the worst of fools.

ambiguities: The actress under discussion (evidently Rachel) is never named in this passage and appears only as "elle"/"une comédienne"; per the reference sheet she has no reviewed unnamed-figure entry, so she is excluded from characters_present and the mockery is instead read as bearing on Robert's judgment by association.
